summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for managing the Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) protocol for IPv4. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: PIM helps deliver one stream to many viewers. This gives tools a way to look at and manage how it is running.

questions: how to monitor pim with snmp
is the pim mib for ipv6
subtitle: The SNMP objects a router exposes so operators can see and configure IPv4 Protocol Independent Multicast.

tldr.problem: Operators need a standard way to inspect and configure Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) on IPv4 multicast routers using network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module, written in SMIv2, with one scalar and eight tables covering interfaces, neighbors, multicast routes, next hops, rendezvous points and PIM components.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental RFC. It covers IPv4 only, and some objects are deprecated because they exist only to manage PIMv1 routers.

today: RFC 2934 is an Experimental RFC from October 2000, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What This MIB Manages
sections.content:
RFC 2934 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) used by network management protocols. It describes managed objects for the Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM) protocol for IPv4, and applies to IPv4 multicast routers that implement PIM.

The MIB does not support management of PIM for other address families, including IPv6. The memo says such management may be supported by other MIBs.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a car dashboard. This memo describes the dashboard for a router that helps send one video to many people at once.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
The memo reviews the five parts of the SNMP Management Framework: an overall architecture, the Structure of Management Information (SMI) for describing objects, message protocols (SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3), protocol operations, and a set of fundamental applications plus view-based access control.

This MIB module is written in SMIv2. A MIB conforming to SMIv1 can be produced through the appropriate translations, and the result must be semantically equivalent except where objects or events are omitted because no translation is possible (use of Counter64).
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is the common language that lets a management program ask routers questions. This memo writes its questions in that language.

sections.title: One Scalar and Eight Tables
sections.content:
The module contains one scalar, pimJoinPruneInterval, the default interval for periodic PIM-SM Join/Prune messages. It also holds eight tables: the Interface, Neighbor, IP Multicast Route, Next Hop, RP, RP-Set, Candidate-RP and Component tables.

Some objects are deprecated. They remain because they are needed to manage PIMv1 routers, but PIMv1 itself is obsoleted by PIMv2.

The Interface table has one row per PIM interface, indexed by pimInterfaceIfIndex. An interface can be in dense, sparse or sparseDense mode, and sparseDense is only valid for PIMv1. Hello messages default to every 30 seconds. Creating a row enables PIM on the interface and destroying it disables PIM.
sections.plainLanguage: The router keeps lists, like a class roster for each kind of thing it knows: its doors, its neighbors, and its routes. The MIB lets you read each roster.

sections.title: Neighbors, Routes and Rendezvous Points
sections.content:
The Neighbor table lists the router's PIM neighbors. The IP Multicast Route table has one row per multicast routing entry whose incoming interface is running PIM. The Next Hop table has one row per outgoing interface list entry whose interface runs PIM and whose state is pruned.

The RP-Set table holds PIMv2 information about sets of candidate Rendezvous Points for group address prefixes. The Candidate-RP table lists the groups for which the local router advertises itself as a Candidate-RP; if it is empty, the router advertises itself for all groups. The Component table has one row for each PIM domain the router is connected to.

A notification, pimNeighborLoss, signals the loss of an adjacency with a neighbor.
sections.plainLanguage: The router can tell you who its neighbors are, which streams pass through, and which meeting-point routers it knows about. It can also send an alert when a neighbor disappears.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Readable objects reveal information about multicast routing, including network topology. Unauthorized access to them is described as relatively innocuous. Unauthorized access to writable objects could cause a denial of service, so SET operations in a non-secure environment can harm network operations.

SNMPv1 by itself is an insecure environment. The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 security features, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 2274) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 2575). Operators must configure the SNMP entity so only legitimate principals can reach these objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Looking at the dashboard is mostly harmless, but letting a stranger turn the dials could break things. So only trusted people should get the keys.

viz.caption: THE EIGHT TABLES IN THE PIM MIB

cells: each PIM interface of the router
each multicast routing entry whose incoming interface runs PIM
each pruned outgoing interface list entry on a PIM interface
PIMv1 information common to all RPs of a group
PIMv2 candidate RP sets per group prefix
groups for which the router advertises itself as Candidate-RP
each PIM domain the router is connected to
